title: The art of conversation
hookLine: he loved a good, sharp conversation and hated flattery (Essays 3.8)
last: EVEN A VIRTUE, GRIPPED TOO HARD, BECOMES A FAULT.

cards: Somebody at the table says something you think is wrong. A few moves are available. Nod and change the subject.

Agree out loud and disagree in the car on the way home. Or say, wait, I don't think that's right, and see what happens. Montaigne knew which one he wanted, from himself and from whoever was talking with him.
He wrote a whole essay about talking, and in it he says he'd rather be contradicted than flattered.

teach.b: First, how much he prized it. In the essay Of the art of conversing, Montaigne calls conversation the most fruitful and natural exercise of our minds.
He finds it sweeter than any other act of life, so much that he'd sooner give up his sight than his hearing or his speech. Second, what he wanted from it. Not agreement.
When someone opposes him, he says, it wakes his attention, not his anger. He moves toward the person who contradicts him, because that person is teaching him.

Truth is welcome from any hand, and he means to give it a cheerful welcome, even when it beats him. Third, what he couldn't stand. Talk where everyone defers and applauds bores him; he calls that kind of company soft.
He wants a friendship strong enough to enjoy sharpness and vigor in the way people talk.
Flattery wastes the whole point: if the other person only agrees, nothing gets tested. Fourth, the hard part.
Much of the essay is about how talk goes wrong: people get heated, stubborn, more attached to winning than to finding out.
His art isn't about being clever. It's about caring more for the truth than for your own side of the table. Sometimes that's one sentence: I see it differently, and here's why.

how: In the essay Of the art of conversing, Montaigne describes welcoming contradiction as a teacher and disliking talk where everyone only agrees; readers often take it as a guide to disagreeing well.

games.q: you're talking with Montaigne and you tell him flatly he's wrong. what does he say happens inside him?
o: he gets angry and digs in.
his attention wakes up, and he moves toward you.
games.why: contradiction rouses his attention, not his anger. he leans toward the one who opposes him, because that person is teaching him.

practice: Bring to mind someone you'll talk to soon, and one thing you've been nodding along to that you see differently. Find the plain, kind sentence that says so.
Then picture their answer, and yourself leaning toward it, curious, the way Montaigne leaned toward whoever contradicted him.

orig.note: Montaigne's French title: the art of conferring, of talking things through.

carryVoice: Your line: honest talk. Truth is welcome from any hand, even the one that beats you. See you tomorrow.
